learn.b: JavaScript is the language of the web. To see what your program is doing, you print messages with console.log(). The text appears in the console, which is like a notebook where your program writes.
learn.code: console.log("Hello, World!");

learn.b: Text goes inside quotes and is called a string. You can use double quotes or single quotes. Numbers have no quotes, and console.log can print them too.
Give console.log several values separated by commas and it prints them on one line with a space between each. Every console.log call starts a new line.
learn.code:
console.log("Score:", 10);
console.log("a", "b", "c");

learn.b: A comment starts with // and is ignored by the computer. It is a note for humans. A semicolon at the end of a statement is the full stop of code. It is good habit to add it.
learn.code:
// this line is only a note
console.log("Hi"); // this prints Hi

qs.q: Which line prints Hello to the console?
qs.why: console.log() is the JavaScript way to print.

qs.q: What does console.log("a", "b") print?
qs.why: Values separated by commas are printed with one space between them.

qs.q: What does this print?
o: Hi and then there on the next line
qs.why: Each console.log call prints on a new line.

qs.q: The computer runs the text after // as code.
qs.why: Everything after // is a comment and is ignored.

qs.q: Match each piece of code to what it is
Type the number that console.log(2 + 3) prints.
qs.why: 2 + 3 is calculated first, then printed.

qs.q: Arrange the lines to print three words, one per line
qs.why: Code runs from top to bottom.

qs.q: Put the steps of running a program in order
items: Read the output in the console

lab.q: Challenge: print exactly Hello, World! using console.log.

lab.why: // starts a one-line comment.

learn.b: A variable stores a value under a name so you can use it later. You create one with let followed by the name, an equals sign and the value.
learn.code:
let score = 0;
console.log(score);

learn.b: A variable made with let can be given a new value later. Write the name, an equals sign and the new value. You do not write let again.

Use const for values that should never be reassigned, like the number of days in a week. If you try to change a const, JavaScript stops with a TypeError. Many programmers use const by default and let only when the value must change.
learn.code:
const DAYS = 7;
// DAYS = 8;  // TypeError!

learn.b: Names can use letters, digits, _ and $, but cannot start with a digit or contain spaces or dashes. They are case-sensitive. The usual style is camelCase, like highScore, where each new word starts with a capital.
learn.code:
let highScore = 99;
let playerName = "Ava";

qs.q: Which keyword makes a variable that can be reassigned later?
qs.why: let allows reassignment, const does not.

qs.q: Which is a valid variable name?
qs.why: Names cannot start with a digit or contain dashes or spaces.

qs.q: What does this print?
qs.why: a becomes 5 + 2 = 7.

qs.q: A variable declared with const can be reassigned to a new value.
qs.why: Reassigning a const causes a TypeError.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
After let x = 4; and then x = 9; what does console.log(x) print?
qs.why: The last assignment wins, so x is 9.

qs.q: Arrange the lines to add 10 to score and print it
qs.why: Declare first, then change, then print.

items: Declare it with let or const

lab.q: Challenge: type the keyword for a variable that must never be reassigned.
lab.why: const locks the variable to its first value.

learn.b: JavaScript has one number type for whole numbers and decimals. Use + - * / for add, subtract, multiply and divide. Division always gives a decimal when needed, so 10 / 4 is 2.5.
learn.code:
console.log(7 + 2); // 9
console.log(10 / 4); // 2.5
console.log(3 * 4); // 12

learn.b: The % operator gives the remainder after division, so 7 % 3 is 1. It is great for checking even numbers (n % 2 is 0). The ** operator means to the power of, so 2 ** 3 is 8.
learn.code:
console.log(7 % 3); // 1
console.log(2 ** 3); // 8

learn.b: Math has helpful tools. Math.round rounds to the nearest whole number, Math.floor rounds down, Math.ceil rounds up. Math.max and Math.min pick the biggest or smallest, Math.sqrt gives the square root and Math.random gives a random decimal from 0 up to but not including 1.
learn.code:
console.log(Math.floor(4.9)); // 4
console.log(Math.ceil(4.1)); // 5
console.log(Math.max(3, 8, 5)); // 8

learn.b: x += 5 means x = x + 5, and x++ adds 1. Decimals are stored in binary, so 0.1 + 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004, not exactly 0.3. Do not compare decimals for exact equality.

qs.q: What is 7 % 3?
qs.why: 7 divided by 3 is 2 remainder 1.

qs.q: What does Math.floor(4.9) give?
qs.why: floor always rounds down.

qs.q: What does this print?
qs.why: Division in JavaScript keeps the decimal part.

qs.q: In JavaScript, 0.1 + 0.2 is exactly 0.3.
qs.why: Binary rounding makes it 0.30000000000000004.

qs.q: Match each operator or function to its job
Type the number that console.log(2 ** 3) prints.
qs.why: 2 to the power of 3 is 2 * 2 * 2 = 8.

qs.why: n += 3 means n = n + 3, so n is 10.

lab.why: Brackets make the addition happen first.

lab.why: Math.floor rounds down to a whole number.

learn.b: A string is a row of characters. text.length tells how many. Each character has an index starting at 0, so text[0] is the first one. Strings are immutable: you cannot change a character in place, you must make a new string.
The + operator joins strings together, which is called concatenation. Be careful: joining a string with a number gives a string, so "5" + 3 is "53".
learn.code:
console.log("Hi" + " " + "Sam"); // Hi Sam
console.log("5" + 3); // 53

learn.b: Backticks let you write a template literal. Inside it, ${ } inserts any value or expression. This is cleaner than many + signs. Template literals can also span several lines.

toUpperCase() and toLowerCase() change letter case. Special characters start with a backslash: \n makes a new line and \" puts a quote inside a string. These methods return a new string and leave the old one unchanged.

qs.q: What is "hello".length?
qs.why: There are 5 characters.

qs.q: Which uses a template literal?
qs.why: Template literals use backticks.

qs.q: What does this print?
qs.why: Index 0 is J and index 4 is S in JavaScript.

qs.q: You can change a letter in a string with s[0] = "X".
qs.why: Strings are immutable.

pairs: inserts a value in a template

qs.q: What does console.log("5" + 3) print?
qs.why: A string plus a number becomes a joined string.

qs.why: Variables first, then the template literal.

items: Make a variable for the name
Make a variable for a number
Write a template literal with backticks

lab.hint: console.log(`Hello, ${name}!`);

lab.why: Join with a space in the middle.

learn.b: A boolean is either true or false (no quotes). Comparison operators give booleans: > < >= <= compare sizes, and === checks equality. Booleans are what if statements use to decide.
learn.code:
console.log(5 > 3); // true
console.log(2 >= 4); // false

learn.b: === is strict equality: both the value and the type must match, so 5 === "5" is false. == is loose and converts types first, so 5 == "5" is true, which can surprise you. Always prefer === and !==.
learn.code:
console.log(5 === "5"); // false
console.log(5 == "5"); // true
console.log(5 !== 6); // true

learn.b: && means AND: both sides must be true. || means OR: at least one side must be true. ! flips a boolean. Use brackets to make the order clear.

When a value is used as a condition, JavaScript treats some values as false: false, 0, "" (empty string), null, undefined and NaN. Almost everything else is true, including "0" and any non-empty string.
learn.code:
console.log(Boolean(0)); // false
console.log(Boolean("hi")); // true

qs.q: What does 5 === "5" give?
qs.why: The types differ (number vs string), so strict equality is false.

qs.q: Which operator means strict not equal?
qs.why: !== is the strict version of not equal.

qs.q: What does this print?
qs.why: == converts the string to a number, === does not.

qs.q: === checks both the value and the type.
qs.why: That is why it is safer than ==.

qs.q: Match each operator to its meaning

qs.why: The right side is false, so AND is false.

learn.b: An if statement runs a block of code only when its condition is true. Add else to run something when it is false. The condition goes in round brackets and the block in curly braces.
Use else if to test several conditions in order. JavaScript runs the first block whose condition is true and skips the rest. The final else is the fallback.
A switch compares one value against several case labels. Each case should end with break, otherwise the code falls through into the next case. default runs when nothing matches.
For a simple choice between two values you can use the ternary operator: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse. It is an expression, so you can print it or store it.

qs.q: Which keyword runs when none of the if conditions are true?
qs.why: else is the fallback branch of an if.

qs.q: What does break do inside a switch case?
o: Stops it falling through to the next case
qs.why: Without break, execution continues into the next case.

qs.q: What does this print?
qs.why: 18 is not >= 30, but it is >= 15, so mild runs.

qs.q: In an if / else if chain, every true branch runs.
qs.why: Only the first true branch runs.

qs.q: Match each keyword to its role
pairs: runs when the condition is true

qs.q: Type the keyword that handles all other values in a switch.
qs.why: default is the catch-all case.

qs.q: Arrange the lines into an if/else that prints pass or fail
qs.why: The else block comes after the closing brace of if.

qs.q: Put these steps of an if/else in order
items: If true, run the if block
If false, move on to else

lab.hint: Use if, else if and else.
lab.why: Three outcomes need an else if chain.

learn.b: A while loop repeats its block as long as the condition is true. JavaScript checks the condition before every round. If it is false the very first time, the body never runs.
Most loops need a counter: set it before the loop, test it in the condition and change it inside the body. If you forget to change it, the condition stays true forever and you get an infinite loop.
break leaves the loop immediately. continue skips the rest of this round and jumps to the next check. while (true) with a break inside is a common way to loop until something happens.
A do...while loop runs the body first and checks the condition afterwards, so it always runs at least once. It is less common but useful when you must do something before you can test.

qs.q: A while loop keeps running as long as its condition is...
qs.why: The body repeats while the condition is true.

qs.q: Which keyword stops a loop immediately?
qs.why: break leaves the loop.

qs.q: What does this print?
qs.why: i starts at 1 and the loop stops when i reaches 4.

qs.q: while (true) with no break runs forever.
qs.why: The condition is always true, so nothing ends the loop.

pairs: repeat while the condition is true

qs.why: The final console.log comes after the loop.

items: Run the body if it was true

lab.q: Challenge: n is set. Use a while loop to print the sum of 1 to n.

learn.b: A for loop packs the counter pattern into one line: for (start; condition; update). The start runs once, the condition is checked before each round and the update runs after each round.
You can start anywhere and step by any amount. Use i-- to count down and i += 2 to jump by two. The variable declared with let inside the loop only exists inside it.
You can put a loop inside another loop. The inner loop runs completely for every round of the outer loop. This is how you build grids and tables.
The for...of loop walks through a string one character at a time, with no counter needed. Use it when you only need the items, and use the normal for loop when you need the index.

qs.q: In what order are the parts of for (a; b; c) used?
o: a is the update, b is the start
a is the start, b is the condition, c is the update
a is the condition, b is the update
qs.why: Start, condition, update.

qs.q: A variable declared with let in the for header can be used after the loop.

learn.b: An array stores many values in one variable. Write them in square brackets separated by commas. The items can be any type, even mixed, and an empty array is just [].
learn.code:
let fruits = ["apple", "pear", "plum"];
let empty = [];

learn.b: Items are numbered from 0, so fruits[0] is the first. The length property tells how many items there are, so the last item is at index length - 1. You can change an item by assigning to its index.
Use a for loop with an index when you need positions, or for...of when you only need the items. Both visit every item in order.

Declaring an array with const only stops you from reassigning the variable to a different array. You can still change the items inside. Arrays can also hold other arrays, which gives a table: grid[1][0] is the first item of the second row.

qs.q: What is the index of the first item in an array?
qs.why: Indexes start at 0.

qs.why: There are three items.

qs.q: What does this print?
qs.why: Index 1 is replaced with Q.

qs.why: const stops reassignment of the variable, not changes to the contents.

qs.q: Match each expression to its meaning

qs.why: Index 2 is the third item.

qs.q: Arrange the lines to add a third fruit and print the length

learn.b: push adds an item to the end and pop removes the last item and returns it. unshift adds to the front and shift removes the first item. These methods change the original array.
indexOf returns the position of an item, or -1 if it is not there. includes returns true or false. Both use strict comparison, so 2 and "2" are different.
learn.code:
let a = ["x", "y", "z"];
console.log(a.indexOf("z")); // 2
console.log(a.indexOf("q")); // -1
console.log(a.includes("y")); // true

learn.b: slice(start, end) returns a new array from start up to but not including end. The original is not changed. Leave out end to go to the finish.
Printing a whole array shows brackets and spaces that vary by environment. join turns an array into a string using any separator you choose, which makes output predictable.

qs.q: What does push do?
o: Adds an item to the end
Adds an item to the front
qs.why: push appends to the end.

qs.q: What does pop return?
qs.why: pop removes and returns the last item.

qs.q: What does this print?
qs.why: slice(1, 3) takes indexes 1 and 2.

qs.why: 7 is at index 2.

learn.b: A function is a named block of code you can run whenever you want. Define it with the function keyword, a name, brackets and a body. Calling it with its name and brackets runs the body.

Parameters are the names listed in the definition, and they act like variables inside the function. Arguments are the actual values you pass when calling it. You can give a parameter a default value with =.

return sends a value back to the place where the function was called and ends the function. A function with no return gives back undefined. Returning is better than printing because you can use the result in more code.
Variables created inside a function exist only inside it. Outside code cannot see them, and each call starts fresh. This keeps functions tidy and stops names from clashing.

qs.q: Which keyword sends a value back from a function?
qs.why: return hands the value back to the caller.

qs.q: In function add(a, b), what are a and b called?
qs.why: Names in the definition are parameters; the values passed in are arguments.

qs.why: f(1) is 2 and f(2) is 3.

learn.b: Arrow functions are a compact way to write functions. They use => between the parameters and the body, and you usually store them in a const. They were added to JavaScript in 2015 and are everywhere in modern code.

If the body is a single expression and you leave out the curly braces, the value is returned automatically. With braces you must write return yourself. With exactly one parameter the brackets are optional.

Functions are values, so you can store one in a variable, pass it to another function or return it. A function written as const f = function() {} is a function expression. Arrow functions are the short form of the same idea.
Arrow functions shine as short inputs to other functions. For example forEach runs your function once for every array item. You will use this idea a lot with map, filter and event handlers later.

qs.q: Which is a valid arrow function?
qs.why: Arrow functions use =>.

qs.q: An arrow function body has no braces. What happens to the value?
qs.why: A single expression body is returned implicitly.

qs.q: What does this print?
qs.why: f(2) is 6, then f(6) is 18.

qs.q: An arrow function with curly braces returns its last expression automatically.
qs.why: With braces you must write return.

qs.q: Match each piece to its meaning
pairs: runs a function for every item

qs.why: 6 times 6 is 36.
